entries.85589268d9860600ef0436669dc211ee29d2d5c9: <div sID="gen21010" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Zech.14" sID="Zech.14"/> <div eID="gen21010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21011" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21012" type="x-p"/> Divers things were foretold, in the two foregoing chapters, which should come to pass "in that day;" this chapter speaks of a "day of the Lord that cometh," a day of his judgment, and ten times in the foregoing chapters, and seven times in this, it is repeated, "in that day;" but what that day is that is here meant is uncertain, and perhaps will be so (as the Jews speak) till Elias comes; whether it refer to the whole period of time from the prophet's days to the days of the Messiah, or to some particular events in that time, or to Christ's coming, and the setting up of his kingdom upon the ruins of the Jewish polity, we cannot determine, but divers passages here seem to look as far forward as gospel-times. Now the "day of the Lord" brings with it both judgment and mercy, mercy to his church, judgment to her enemies and persecutors. I. The gates of hell are here threatening the church (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.1-Zech.14.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>) and yet not prevailing. II. The power of Heaven appears here for the church and against the enemies of it, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.3">ver. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.5">5</reference>. III. The events concerning the church are here represented as mixed (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.6-Zech.14.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>), but issuing well at last. IV. The spreading of the means of knowledge is here foretold, and the setting up of the gospel-kingdom in the world (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.8-Zech.14.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>), which shall be the enlargement and establishment of another Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.10-Zech.14.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. V. Those shall be reckoned with that fought against Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.12-Zech.14.15">ver. 12-15</reference>) and those that neglect his worship there, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.17-Zech.14.19">ver. 17-19</reference>. VI. It is promised that there shall be great resort to the church, and great purity and piety in it, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">ver. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.20">20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.21">21</reference>.
entries.b89518f28c6113016817fd5970c023313bdd0295: <div eID="gen21012" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21011" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Persecution of the Church; Judgments and Mercies; Encouraging Prospects. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  500.)</title> <div sID="gen21013" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Behold, the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> cometh, and thy spoil shall be divided in the midst of thee. <hi type="super">2</hi> For I will gather all nations against Jerusalem to battle; and the city shall be taken, and the houses rifled, and the women ravished; and half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the residue of the people shall not be cut off from the city. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then shall the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> go forth, and fight against those nations, as when he fought in the day of battle. <hi type="super">4</hi> And his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> before Jerusalem on the east, and the mount of Olives shall cleave in the midst thereof toward the east and toward the west, <hi type="italic">and there shall be</hi> a very great valley; and half of the mountain shall remove toward the north, and half of it toward the south. <hi type="super">5</hi> And ye shall flee <hi type="italic">to</hi> the valley of the mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach unto Azal: yea, ye shall flee, like as ye fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> my God shall come, <hi type="italic">and</hi> all the saints with thee. <hi type="super">6</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the light shall not be clear, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> dark: <hi type="super">7</hi> But it shall be one day which shall be known to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , not day, nor night: but it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> at evening time it shall be light. <div eID="gen21013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21014" type="x-p"/> God's providences concerning his church are here represented as strangely changing and strangely mixed. <div eID="gen21014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21015" type="x-p"/> I. As strangely changing. Sometimes the tide runs high and strong against them, but presently it turns, and comes to be in favour of them; and God has, for wise and holy ends, set the one over against the other. <div eID="gen21015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21016" type="x-p"/> 1. God here appears against Jerusalem; judgment begins at the house of God. When the <hi type="italic">day of the Lord comes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.1">v. 1</reference>) Jerusalem must pass through the fire to be refined. God himself <hi type="italic">gathers all nations against Jerusalem to battle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">v. 2</reference>); he gives them a charge, as he did Sennacherib, to <hi type="italic">take the spoil</hi> and to <hi type="italic">take the prey</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa. x. 6</reference>), for the people of Jerusalem have now become the <hi type="italic">people of his wrath.</hi> And who can stand before him or before nations gathered by him? Where he gives commission he will give success. The <hi type="italic">city shall be taken by the</hi> Romans, who have <hi type="italic">nations</hi> at command; the houses shall be rifled, and all the riches of them taken away, by the enemy; and, to gratify an insatiable lust of uncleanness as well as avarice, <hi type="italic">the women</hi> shall <hi type="italic">be ravished,</hi> as if victory were a license to the worst of villanies, <hi type="italic">jusque datum sceleri—and crimes were sanctioned by law. One-half of the city</hi> shall then be carried <hi type="italic">into captivity,</hi> to be sold or enslaved, and shall not be able to help itself, such is the destruction that shall be made in the great and terrible <hi type="italic">day of the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen21016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21017" type="x-p"/> 2. He presently changes his way, and appears for Jerusalem; for, though judgment begin at the house of God, yet, as it shall not end there, so it shall not make a full end there, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.27">Jer. iv. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">xxx. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen21017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21018" type="x-p"/> (1.) A remnant shall be spared, the same with that <hi type="italic">third part</hi> spoken of, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">ch. xiii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">One-half shall go into captivity,</hi> whence they may hereafter be fetched back, <hi type="italic">and the residue of the people shall not</hi> be cut off, as one would have feared, <hi type="italic">from the city.</hi> Many of the Jews shall receive the gospel, and so shall prevent their being cut off from the city of God, his church upon earth. <hi type="italic">In it shall be a tenth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Isa. vi. 13</reference>; See <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.3">Ezek. v. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen21018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21019" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their cause shall be pleaded against their enemies (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then,</hi> when God has made use of these nations as a scourge to his people, he shall <hi type="italic">go forth</hi> and <hi type="italic">fight against them</hi> by his judgments, <hi type="italic">as when he fought</hi> against the enemies of his church formerly <hi type="italic">in the day of battle,</hi> with the Egyptians, Canaanites, and others. Note, The instruments of God's wrath will themselves be made the objects of it; for it will come to their turn to drink of the cup of trembling; and whom God fights against he will be sure to overcome and be too hard for. And every former <hi type="italic">day of battle,</hi> which God has made to his people a <hi type="italic">day of triumph,</hi> as it is an engagement to God to appear for his people, because he is the same, so it is an encouragement to them to trust in him. It is observable that the Roman empire never flourished, after the destruction of Jerusalem as it had done before, but in many instances God fought against it. <div eID="gen21019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21020" type="x-p"/> (3.) Though Jerusalem and the temple be destroyed, yet God will have a church in the world, into which Gentiles shall be admitted, and with whom the believing Jews shall be incorporated, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.4-Zech.14.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. These verses are dark and hard to be understood; but divers good expositors take this to be the meaning of them. [1.] God will carefully inspect Jerusalem, even then when the enemies of it are laying it waste: <hi type="italic">His feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives,</hi> whence he may take a full view of the city and temple, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.3">Mark xiii. 3</reference>. When the refiner puts his gold into the furnace he stands by it, and has his eye upon it, to see that it receive no damage; so when Jerusalem, God's gold, is to be refined, he will have the oversight of it. He will stand by <hi type="italic">upon the mount of Olives;</hi> this was literally fulfilled when our Lord Jesus was often upon this mountain, especially when thence he <hi type="italic">ascended up into heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.12">Acts i. 12</reference>. It was the last place on which his feet stood on this earth, the place from which he took rise. [2.] The partition-wall between Jews and Gentiles shall be taken away. The <hi type="italic">mountains about Jerusalem,</hi> and particularly this, signified it to be an enclosure, and that it stood in the way of those who would approach to it. Between the Gentiles and Jerusalem this <hi type="italic">mountain of Bether,</hi> of <hi type="italic">division,</hi> stood, <reference osisRef="Song.2.17">Cant. ii. 17</reference>. But by the destruction of Jerusalem this mountain shall be made to <hi type="italic">cleave in the midst,</hi> and so the Jewish pale shall be taken down, and the church laid in common with the Gentiles, who were made one with the Jews by the breaking down of this <hi type="italic">middle wall of partition,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Eph. ii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who art thou, O great mountain?</hi> And a great mountain the ceremonial law was in the way of the Jews' conversion, which, one would think, could never have been got over; yet before Christ and his gospel it was made plain. This <hi type="italic">mountain departs,</hi> this <hi type="italic">hill removes,</hi> but the <hi type="italic">covenant of peace</hi> cannot be <hi type="italic">broken;</hi> for peace is still <hi type="italic">preached to him that is afar off and to those that are nigh.</hi> [3.] A new and living way shall be opened to the new Jerusalem, both to see it and to come into it. The mountain being divided, one-half <hi type="italic">towards the north</hi> and the other half <hi type="italic">towards the south,</hi> there shall be <hi type="italic">a very great valley,</hi> that is, a broad way of communication opened between Jerusalem and the Gentile world, by which the Gentiles shall have free admission into the gospel-Jerusalem, and the word of the Lord, that <hi type="italic">goes forth from Jerusalem,</hi> shall have a <hi type="italic">free course</hi> into the Gentile world. Thus the <hi type="italic">way of the Lord</hi> is prepared, for <hi type="italic">every mountain and hill shall be brought low,</hi> and plain and pleasant valleys shall come in the room of them, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.4">Isa. xl. 4</reference>. [4.] Those of the Jews that believe shall come in, and join themselves to the Gentiles, and incorporate with them in the gospel-church: <hi type="italic">You shall flee to the valley of the mountains,</hi> that valley that is opened between the divided halves of the mount of Olives; they shall hasten into the church with the Gentiles, as formerly the Gentiles with them, <reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">ch. viii. 23</reference>. The <hi type="italic">valley of the mountains</hi> is the gospel-church, to which there were added of the Jews daily <hi type="italic">such as should be saved,</hi> who fled to that valley as to their refuge. This <hi type="italic">valley of the mountains</hi> is said to <hi type="italic">reach unto Azal,</hi> or <hi type="italic">to the separate place,</hi> that is, to all those whom God has <hi type="italic">set apart for himself.</hi> When God <hi type="italic">makes his mountains a way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.11">Isa. xlix. 11</reference>), by making them a valley, the way shall be opened to all the <hi type="italic">way-faring men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>), and, <hi type="italic">though fools,</hi> they <hi type="italic">shall not err therein.</hi> Or, to those that are now separated from God this valley shall reach; for the Gentiles, who are afar off, shall be made nigh, with the Jews, who are a <hi type="italic">people near unto him,</hi> and both have <hi type="italic">an access,</hi> a mutual access to each other and a joint access to God as a Father by one Spirit, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.18">Eph. ii. 18</reference>. [5.] They shall flee to <hi type="italic">the valley of the mountains,</hi> to the gospel-church, under dreadful apprehensions of their danger from the curse of the law. They shall <hi type="italic">flee from the wrath to come,</hi> from the avenger of blood, who is in pursuit of them, to the church as to a <hi type="italic">city of refuge,</hi> or <hi type="italic">as doves to their windows,</hi> as they <hi type="italic">fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Amos i. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> the gospel reveals the wrath of God from heaven (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.18">Rom. i. 18</reference>) that we might be awakened to <hi type="italic">escape for our lives,</hi> to flee as from an earthquake, for we feel the earth ready to sink under us, and we can find no firm footing in it, and therefore must flee to Christ, in whom alone we can stand fast and be easy. <div eID="gen21020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21021" type="x-p"/> (4.) God shall appear in his glory for the accomplishing of all this: <hi type="italic">The Lord my God shall come, and all the saints with thee,</hi> which may refer to his coming to destroy Jerusalem, or to destroy the enemies of Jerusalem, or his coming to set up his kingdom in the world, which is called the <hi type="italic">coming of the Son of man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.37">Matt. xxiv. 37</reference>), or to his last coming, at the end of time; however, it teaches us, [1.] That the Lord will come; it has been the faith of all the saints, <hi type="italic">Behold, the Lord comes</hi> to fulfil every word that he has spoken in its season. [2.] When he comes all his saints come with him; they attend his motions and are ready to serve his interests. Christ will come at the end of time with <hi type="italic">ten thousands of his saints,</hi> as when he came to give the law upon Mount Sinai. [3.] Every particular believer, being related to God as his God, may triumph in the expectation of his coming and speak of it with pleasure, <hi type="italic">The Lord my God shall come,</hi> shall come to the comfort of all that are his; for, "Blessed Lord, <hi type="italic">all the saints shall be with thee,</hi> and it shall be their everlasting happiness to dwell in thy presence; and therefore <hi type="italic">come, Lord Jesus.</hi>" And some think that this may be read as a prayer, <hi type="italic">Yet, O Lord my God! come, and bring all the saints with thee.</hi> <div eID="gen21021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21022" type="x-p"/> II. God's providences appear here strangely mixed (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.6-Zech.14.7">v. 6, 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">In that day</hi> of the Lord the <hi type="italic">light shall not be clear nor dark, not day</hi> nor <hi type="italic">night;</hi> but <hi type="italic">at evening time it shall be light.</hi> Some refer this to all the time from hence to the coming of the Messiah; the Jewish church had neither perfect peace nor constant trouble, but a cloudy day, neither rain nor sunshine. But it may be taken more generally, as designed to represent the method God usually takes in the administration of the kingdom both of providence and grace. Here is, 1. An idea of the usual course and tenour of God's dispensations; the day of his grace and the day of his providence are <hi type="italic">neither clear nor dark, not day nor night.</hi> It is so with the church of God in this world; where the Sun of righteousness has risen it cannot be dark night, and yet short of heaven it will not be clear day. It is so with particular saints; they are not darkness, but <hi type="italic">light in the Lord,</hi> and yet, while there is so much error and corruption remaining in them, it is not perfect day. So it is as to the providences of God that relate to his church; in general the affairs of the church are neither good nor bad in any extremity, but there is a mixture of both; we are singing both of mercy and judgment, and are uncertain which will prevail, whether it be an evening or a morning twilight. We are between hope and fear, not knowing what to make of things. 2. An intimation of comfort with reference hereunto: <hi type="italic">It shall be one day which shall be known to the Lord.</hi> This intimates, (1.) The beauty and harmony of such mixed events; there is one and the same design and tendency in all; all the wheels make but one wheel, all the revolutions but one day. (2.) The brevity of them; it is, as it were, but for one day, for a little moment; the cloud that darkens the light will soon blow over. (3.) The eye God has upon all these events, and the hand he has in them all; they are <hi type="italic">known to the Lord;</hi> he takes notice of them, and orders and disposes of all for the best, according to the counsel of his will. 3. An issue very joyful secured at last: <hi type="italic">At evening-time it shall be light:</hi> it shall be clear light, and no longer dark; we are sure of it in the other world, and we hope for it in this world—at <hi type="italic">evening-time,</hi> when our hopes are quite spent with waiting all day to no purpose, nay, when we fear it will be quite dark, when things are at the worst and the case of the church is most deplorable. As to the church's enemies <hi type="italic">the sun goes down at noon,</hi> so to the church it rises at night; unto the upright springs <hi type="italic">light out of darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">Ps. cxii. 4</reference>); deliverance comes when the tale of bricks is doubled, and when God's people have done looking for it, and so it comes with a pleasing surprise.
entries.eb9379366cd9ee41a89cc3a090d4c8cd8388cf58: <div eID="gen21022" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Blessings Promised to the Church; Judgments Threatened. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 500.)</title> <div sID="gen21023" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And it shall be in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> living waters shall go out from Jerusalem; half of them toward the former sea, and half of them toward the hinder sea: in summer and in winter shall it be. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and his name one. <hi type="super">10</hi> All the land shall be turned as a plain from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem: and it shall be lifted up, and inhabited in her place, from Benjamin's gate unto the place of the first gate, unto the corner gate, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> the tower of Hananeel unto the king's wine-presses. <hi type="super">11</hi> And <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall dwell in it, and there shall be no more utter destruction; but Jerusalem shall be safely inhabited. <hi type="super">12</hi> And this shall be the plague wherewith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will smite all the people that have fought against Jerusalem; Their flesh shall consume away while they stand upon their feet, and their eyes shall consume away in their holes, and their tongue shall consume away in their mouth. <hi type="super">13</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> a great tumult from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be among them; and they shall lay hold every one on the hand of his neighbour, and his hand shall rise up against the hand of his neighbour. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Judah also shall fight at Jerusalem; and the wealth of all the heathen round about shall be gathered together, gold, and silver, and apparel, in great abundance. <hi type="super">15</hi> And so shall be the plague of the horse, of the mule, of the camel, and of the ass, and of all the beasts that shall be in these tents, as this plague. <div eID="gen21023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21024" type="x-p"/> Here are, I. Blessings promised to Jerusalem, the gospel-Jerusalem, in the day of the Messiah, and to all the earth, by virtue of the blessings poured out on Jerusalem, especially to the land of Israel. <div eID="gen21024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21025" type="x-p"/> 1. Jerusalem shall be a spring of living waters to the world; it was made so when there the Spirit was poured out upon the apostles, and thence the word of the Lord diffused itself to the nations about (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Living waters shall go out from Jerusalem;</hi> for there they began, and thence those set out who were to preach <hi type="italic">repentance</hi> and <hi type="italic">remission</hi> of sins <hi type="italic">unto all nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Luke xxiv. 47</reference>. Note, Where the gospel goes, and the graces of God's Spirit go along with it, there living waters go; those streams that <hi type="italic">make glad the city of our God</hi> make glad the country also, and make it like paradise, like the <hi type="italic">garden of the Lord,</hi> which was <hi type="italic">well watered.</hi> It was the honour of Jerusalem that <hi type="italic">thence the word of the Lord went forth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>); and thus far, even in its worst and most degenerate age, for old acquaintance-sake, it was made a blessing, and to be so is to be blessed. Half of these waters shall go <hi type="italic">towards the former sea</hi> and <hi type="italic">half towards the hinder sea,</hi> as all rivers bend their course towards some sea or other, some eastward, others westward. The gospel shall spread into all parts of the world, into some that lie remote from Jerusalem one way and others that lie as far off another way; for the dominion of the Redeemer, which was thereby to be set up, must be <hi type="italic">from sea to sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">Ps. lxxii. 8</reference>), and the earth must be <hi type="italic">full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea,</hi> and as the waters that in various channels run to the sea. The knowledge of God shall diffuse itself, (1.) Every way. These living waters shall produce both eastern churches and western churches, that shall each of them in its turn be illustrious. (2.) Every day: In <hi type="italic">summer and in winter it shall be.</hi> Note, Those who are employed in spreading the gospel may find themselves work both <hi type="italic">winter</hi> and <hi type="italic">summer,</hi> and are to serve the Lord therein at all seasons, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.18">Acts xx. 18</reference>. And such a divine power goes along with these living waters that they shall not be dried up, nor the course of them be obstructed, either by the droughts in summer or by the frosts in winter. <div eID="gen21025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21026" type="x-p"/> 2. The kingdom of God among men shall be a universal and united kingdom, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.9">v. 9</reference>. (1.) It shall be a universal kingdom: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall be King over all the earth.</hi> He is, and ever was, so of right, and in the sovereign disposals of his providence his kingdom does <hi type="italic">rule over all</hi> and none are exempt from his jurisdiction; but it is here promised that he shall be so by actual possession of the hearts of his subjects; he shall be acknowledged King by all in all places; his authority shall be owned and submitted to, and allegiance sworn to him. This will have its accomplishment with that word (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Rev. xi. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">The kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ.</hi> (2.) It shall be a united kingdom: <hi type="italic">There shall be one Lord, and his name one.</hi> All shall worship one God only, and not idols, and shall be unanimous in the worship of him. All false gods shall be abandoned, and all false ways of worship abolished; and as God shall be the centre of their unity, in whom they shall all meet, so the scripture shall be the rule of their unity, by which they shall all walk. <div eID="gen21026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21027" type="x-p"/> 3. The land of Judea, and Jerusalem, its mother-city, shall be repaired and replenished, and taken under the special protection of Heaven, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.10-Zech.14.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Some think this denotes particular favour to the people of the Jews, and points at their conversion and restoration in the latter days; but it is rather to be understood figuratively of the gospel-church, typified by Judah and Jerusalem, and it signifies the abundant graces with which the church shall be crowned, and the fruitfulness of its members, and the vast numbers of them. (1.) The church shall be like a fruitful country, abounding in all the rich products of the soil. The whole land of Judea, which is naturally uneven and hilly, shall be <hi type="italic">turned as a plain;</hi> it shall become a smooth level valley, from Geba, or Gibeah, its utmost border north, to Rimmon, which lay <hi type="italic">south of Jerusalem</hi> and was the utmost southern limit of Judea. The gospel of Christ, where it comes in its power, levels the ground; mountains and hills are brought low by it, that the Lord alone may be exalted. (2.) It shall be like a populous city. As the holy land shall be levelled, so the holy city shall be peopled, shall be rebuilt and replenished. <hi type="italic">Jerusalem shall be lifted</hi> up out of its low estate, shall be raised out of its ruins; when <hi type="italic">the land is turned as a plain,</hi> and not only the <hi type="italic">mount of Olives</hi> removed (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.4">v. 4</reference>), but other mountains too, then Jerusalem shall be <hi type="italic">lifted up,</hi> that is, shall appear the more conspicuous; she <hi type="italic">shall be inhabited in her place,</hi> even <hi type="italic">in Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.12.6">ch. xii. 6</reference>. The whole city shall be inhabited in the utmost extent of it, and no part of it left to lie waste. The utmost limits of it are here mentioned, between which there shall be no ground lost, but all built upon, from <hi type="italic">Benjamin's-gate</hi> north-east to the <hi type="italic">corner-gate</hi> north-west, and <hi type="italic">from the tower of Hananeel</hi> in the south to the <hi type="italic">king's wine-presses</hi> in the north; when the churches of Christ in all places are replenished with great numbers of holy, humble, serious Christians, and many such are daily added to it, then this promise is fulfilled. (3.) This country and this city shall both be safe, both the meat in the country and the mouths in the city: <hi type="italic">Those that dwell in it</hi> shall dwell securely, and there shall be none to make them afraid; there shall be no more of that utter destruction that has laid both town and country waste, no more anathema (as some read it), no more cutting off, no more curse, or separation from God to evil, no more such desolating judgments as you have been groaning under, but Jerusalem <hi type="italic">shall be safely inhabited;</hi> there shall be no danger, nor any apprehension of it; neither shall its friends be fearful to disquiet themselves nor its enemies formidable to disquiet them. That promise of Christ explains this—that <hi type="italic">the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church;</hi> and so do the holy security and serenity of mind which believers enjoy in relying on the divine protection. <div eID="gen21027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21028" type="x-p"/> II. Here are judgments threatened against the enemies of the church, that <hi type="italic">have fought,</hi> or do fight, against Jerusalem; and the <hi type="italic">threatening of these</hi> judgments is in order to the preservation of the church in safety. Men that read and hear of these plagues will be afraid of fighting against Jerusalem, much more when these threatenings are fulfilled in some will others hear and fear. Those that fight against the city of God, and his people, will be found fighting against God, against whom none ever hardened his heart and prospered (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">This shall be the plague wherewith the Lord will smite all the people that have fought against Jerusalem;</hi> whoever they are, God will punish them for the affront done to him, and avenge Jerusalem upon them. 1. They shall waste away under grievous and languishing diseases: <hi type="italic">Their flesh shall consume away,</hi> and they shall be miserably emaciated, even <hi type="italic">while they stand on their feet,</hi> so that they shall be walking skeletons; nothing shall remain but skin and bones. The flesh which they pampered and indulged, and made provision for, when they were fed to the full with the spoils of God's people, shall now <hi type="italic">consume away, that it cannot be seen, and the bones that were not seen shall stick out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.21">Job xxxiii. 21</reference>. They <hi type="italic">keep their feet,</hi> and hope to <hi type="italic">keep their ground,</hi> crawling about as long as they can; but they must yield at last. The organs of sight, the outlets of sin, <hi type="italic">their eyes, shall consume away in their holes,</hi> shall sink into their heads or perhaps start out of them; their envious malicious, adulterous eyes, the eyes they had so often fed with spectacles of misery, these shall consume, which shall make not only their countenances ghastly, but their lives wretched. The organs of speech, the outlets of sin, <hi type="italic">their tongue, shall consume away in their mouth,</hi> whereby God will reckon with them for all their blasphemies against himself and invectives against his people. Thus <hi type="italic">their own tongues shall fall upon them,</hi> and their punishment shall be legible in their sin, as his was whose tongue was tormented in hell-flames. Thus Antiochus and Herod consumed away. 2. They shall be dashed in pieces one against another (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">A great tumult from the Lord shall be among them.</hi> But are tumults from the Lord, who is the <hi type="italic">God of order, and not of confusion?</hi> As they are the sin of those that raise them they are not from the Lord, but from the wicked one, and from men's own lusts; but, as they are the punishment of those that suffer by them, they are from the Lord, who serves his own purposes, and carries on his intentions, by the sins, and follies, and restless spirits, of men. It is of themselves that they <hi type="italic">bite and devour one another,</hi> but it is of the Lord, the righteous Judge, that thus they are <hi type="italic">consumed one of another</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.15">Gal. v. 15</reference>); as Ahab was deceived by a lying spirit from the Lord, so Abimelech and the men of Shechem were <hi type="italic">divided,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">destroyed,</hi> by an <hi type="italic">evil spirit from the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.9.23">Judg. ix. 23</reference>. Note, Those that are confederate and combined against the church will justly be separated, and set against one another; and their tumults raised against God will be avenged in tumults among themselves. And they shall <hi type="italic">lay hold every one on the hand of his neighbour,</hi> to hold him from striking, or to bind him as his prisoner; nay, <hi type="italic">his hand shall rise up against the hand of his neighbour,</hi> to strike and wound him. Note, Those that aim to destroy the church are often made to destroy one another; and every man's sword is sometimes set against his fellow, by him whose sword they all are. Some think this was fulfilled in the factions and dissensions that were among the Jews, when the Romans were destroying them all; for they had fought against the spiritual Jerusalem, the gospel-church; and to that well enough agrees <reference osisRef="Zech.14.14">v. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou also, O Judah! shalt fight against Jerusalem;</hi> the Jewish nation shall be ruined by itself, shall die by its own hands; the city and country shall be at war with each other, and so both shall be destroyed. <hi type="italic">Suis et ipsa Roma viribus ruit—Rome was urged into ruin by its very strength.</hi> 3. The plunder of their camp shall greatly enrich the people of God, or the spoils of their country (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Judah also shall eat at Jerusalem</hi> (so one learned interpreter reads it); people shall come from all parts to share in the prey; as when Sennacherib's army was routed before Jerusalem there was <hi type="italic">the prey of a great spoil divided</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.23">Isa. xxxiii. 23</reference>), so it shall be now; the <hi type="italic">wealth of all the heathen round about,</hi> that had spoiled <hi type="italic">Jerusalem, shall be gathered together, gold, and silver, and apparel, in great abundance,</hi> that an equal dividend may be made among all the parties entitled to a share of the prize. Note, The <hi type="italic">wealth of the sinner is</hi> often <hi type="italic">laid up for the just,</hi> and the Israel of God enriched with the spoil of the Egyptians. 4. The very cattle shall share in the plague with which the enemies of God's church shall be cut off, as they did in divers of the plagues of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.15">v. 15</reference>): All <hi type="italic">the beasts</hi> that <hi type="italic">shall be in the tents</hi> of these wicked men, when God comes to contend with them, shall perish with them, not only beasts used in war, as the horse, but those used for travel, or in the plough, as the <hi type="italic">mule,</hi> the <hi type="italic">camel,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">ass.</hi> Note, The inferior creatures often suffer for the sin of man and in his plagues. Thus God will show his indignation against sin, and will make the creature that is thus <hi type="italic">subject to vanity</hi> groan to be <hi type="italic">delivered</hi> into the glorious liberty of the children of God, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.21-Rom.8.22">Rom. viii. 21, 22</reference>.
entries.d712c5e27475778d3b436b97586d4022cf410cb4: <div eID="gen21028" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Evangelical Predictions; Threatenings and Promises; Encouraging Prospects. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  500.)</title> <div sID="gen21029" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> every one that is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall even go up from year to year to worship the King, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, and to keep the feast of tabernacles. <hi type="super">17</hi> And it shall be, <hi type="italic">that</hi> whoso will not come up of <hi type="italic">all</hi> the families of the earth unto Jerusalem to worship the King, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, even upon them shall be no rain. <hi type="super">18</hi> And if the family of Egypt go not up, and come not, that <hi type="italic">have</hi> no <hi type="italic">rain;</hi> there shall be the plague, wherewith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will smite the heathen that come not up to keep the feast of tabernacles. <hi type="super">19</hi> This shall be the punishment of Egypt, and the punishment of all nations that come not up to keep the feast of tabernacles. <hi type="super">20</hi> In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD; and the pots in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house shall be like the bowls before the altar. <hi type="super">21</hi> Yea, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah shall be holiness unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts: and all they that sacrifice shall come and take of them, and seethe therein: and in that day there shall be no more the Canaanite in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <div eID="gen21029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21030" type="x-p"/> Three things are here foretold:— <div eID="gen21030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21031" type="x-p"/> I. That a gospel-way of worship being set up in the church there shall be a great resort to it and a general attendance upon it. Those that were left of the enemies of religion shall be so sensible of the mercy of God to them in their narrow escape that they shall apply themselves to the worship of the God of Israel, and pay their homage to him, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">v. 16</reference>. Those that were not consumed shall be converted, and this makes their deliverance a mercy indeed, a double mercy. It is a great change that the grace of God makes upon them; those that had <hi type="italic">come against Jerusalem,</hi> finding their attempts vain and fruitless, shall become as much her admirers as ever they had been her adversaries, and shall <hi type="italic">come to Jerusalem</hi> to worship there, and go in concurrence with those whom they had gone contrary to. Note, As some of Christ's foes shall be made his footstool, so others of them shall be made his friends; and, when the principle of enmity is slain in them, their former acts of hostility are pardoned to them, and their services are admitted and accepted, as though they had never <hi type="italic">fought against Jerusalem.</hi> They shall <hi type="italic">go up to worship</hi> at Jerusalem, because that was the place which God had chosen, and there the temple was, which was a type of Christ and his mediation. Converting grace sets us right, 1. In the object of our worship. <hi type="italic">They shall</hi> no longer <hi type="italic">worship</hi> the Molochs and Baals, the <hi type="italic">kings</hi> and <hi type="italic">lords,</hi> that the Gentiles worship, the creatures of their own imagination, but <hi type="italic">the King,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> the everlasting King, the King of kings, the sovereign Lord of all. 2. In the ordinances of worship, those which God himself has appointed. Gospel-worship is here represented by the <hi type="italic">keeping of the feast of tabernacles,</hi> for the sake of those two great graces which were in a special manner <hi type="italic">acted</hi> and <hi type="italic">signified</hi> in that feast-contempt of the world, and joy in God, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.17">Neh. viii. 17</reference>. The life of a good Christian is a constant <hi type="italic">feast of tabernacles,</hi> and, in all acts of devotion, we must retire from the world and rejoice in the Lord, must worship as in that feast. 3. In the <hi type="italic">Mediator</hi> of our worship; we must go to Christ our temple with all our offerings, for in him only our <hi type="italic">spiritual sacrifices</hi> are acceptable to God, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1 Pet. ii. 5</reference>. If we rest in ourselves, we come short of pleasing God; we must go up to him, and mention his righteousness only. 4. In the time of it; we must be constant. They shall go up <hi type="italic">from year to year,</hi> at the times appointed for this solemn feast. Every day of a Christian's life is a day of the <hi type="italic">feast of tabernacles,</hi> and every Lord's day especially (that is the <hi type="italic">great day of the feast</hi>); and therefore every day we must worship the Lord of hosts and every Lord's day with a peculiar solemnity. <div eID="gen21031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21032" type="x-p"/> II. That those who neglect the duties of gospel-worship shall be reckoned with for their neglect. God will compel them to come and worship before him, by suspending his favours from those that keep not his ordinances: <hi type="italic">Upon them there shall be no rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.14.17">v. 17</reference>. Some understand it figuratively; the rain of heavenly doctrine shall be withheld, and of the heavenly grace, which should accompany that doctrine. God will <hi type="italic">command the clouds that they rain no rain upon them.</hi> Note, It is a righteous thing with God to withhold the blessings of grace from those that do not attend the means of grace, to deny the <hi type="italic">green pastures</hi> to those that attend not the <hi type="italic">shepherd's tents.</hi> Or we may take it literally: <hi type="italic">On them there shall be no rain,</hi> to make their ground fruitful. Note, The gifts of common providence are justly denied to those that neglect and despise instituted ordinances. Those that neglected to build the temple were punished with the want of rain (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.17">Hag. ii. 17</reference>), and so were those that neglected to attend there when it was built. If we be barren and unfruitful towards God, justly is the earth made so to us. Many are crossed, and go backward, in their affairs, and this is at the bottom of it—they do not keep close to the worship of God as they should; they go off from God, and then he walks contrary to them. If we omit or postpone the duties he expects from us, it is just with him to deny the favours we expect from him. But what shall be done to the defaulters of the land of Egypt, to whom the threatening of the want of rain is no threatening, for they have no rain at any time; they need none; they desire none; the river Nilus is to them instead of the clouds of heaven, waters their land, and makes it fruitful, so that what is a punishment to others is none to them? <reference osisRef="Zech.14.18-Zech.14.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. It is threatened that <hi type="italic">if the family of Egypt go not up, that have no rain,</hi> yet God will find out a way to meet with them, for there shall be, in effect, the same plague wherewith other nations are smitten for their neglect. God can, and often did, restrain the overflowing of the river, which was equivalent to the shutting up of the clouds; or if the river did its part, and rose as high as it used to do, God had other ways of bringing famine upon them, and destroying the fruits of their ground, as he did by several of the ten plagues of Egypt, so that <hi type="italic">this</hi> (that is, the same) shall be <hi type="italic">the punishment of Egypt</hi> that is the punishment of other <hi type="italic">nations</hi> who come not up to <hi type="italic">keep the feast of tabernacles.</hi> Note, Those who think themselves least indebted to, and depending on, the mercy of heaven, cannot <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> think themselves guarded against the justice of Heaven. It does not follow that those who can live without rain can therefore live without God; for not the heavens only, but all other creatures, are that to us that God makes them to be, and no more; nor can any man's way of living enable him to set light by the judgments of God. This shall be the <hi type="italic">punishment</hi>—margin, <hi type="italic">This shall be the sin of Egypt, and the sin of all nations, that come not up to keep the feast of tabernacles.</hi> The same word signifies both <hi type="italic">sin</hi> and the <hi type="italic">punishment</hi> of sin, so close and inseparable is the connexion between them (as <reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen. iv. 7</reference>), and sin is often its own punishment. Note, Omissions are sins, and we must come into judgment for them; those contract guilt that <hi type="italic">go not up to worship</hi> at the times appointed, as they have opportunity; and it is a sin that is its own <hi type="italic">punishment,</hi> for those who forsake the duty forfeit the privilege of communion with God. <div eID="gen21032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21033" type="x-p"/> III. That those who perform the duties of gospel-worship shall have grace to adorn their profession by the duties of a gospel-conversation too. This is promised (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.20-Zech.14.21">v. 20, 21</reference>), and it is necessary to the completing of the beauty and happiness of the church. In general, all shall be <hi type="italic">holiness to the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen21033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21034" type="x-p"/> 1. The name and character of holiness shall not be so confined as formerly. <hi type="italic">Holiness to the Lord</hi> had been written only upon the high priest's forehead, but now it shall not be so appropriated. All Christians shall be <hi type="italic">living temples,</hi> and <hi type="italic">spiritual priests,</hi> dedicated to the honour of God and employed in his service. <div eID="gen21034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21035" type="x-p"/> 2. Real holiness shall be more diffused than it had been, because there shall be more powerful means of sanctification, more excellent rules, more cogent arguments, and brighter patterns of holiness, and because there shall be a more plentiful effusion of the Spirit of holiness and sanctification, after Christ's ascension than ever before. <div eID="gen21035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21036" type="x-p"/> (1.) There shall be holiness introduced into common things; and those things shall be devoted to God that seemed very foreign. [1.] The furniture of their horses shall be consecrated to God. "<hi type="italic">Upon the bells of the horses</hi> shall be engraven <hi type="italic">Holiness to the Lord,</hi> or upon the <hi type="italic">bridles</hi> of the horses (so the margin) or the <hi type="italic">trappings.</hi> The horses used in war shall no longer be used against God and his people, as they have been, but for him and them. Even their wars shall be holy wars, their troopers serving under God's banner. Their great men, who ride in state with a pompous retinue, shall reckon it their greatest ornament to honour God with their honours. <hi type="italic">Holiness to the Lord</hi> shall be written on the harness of their chariot-horses, as great men have sometimes their coat of arms with their motto painted on their coaches; every gentleman shall take the high priest's motto for his, and glory in it, and make it a memento to himself not to do any thing unworthy of it. Travellers shall have it upon their bridles, with which they guide their horses, as those who desire always to be put in mind of it, by having it continually before them, and to guide themselves in all their motions by this rule. The <hi type="italic">bells of the horses,</hi> which are designed to quicken them in their journey and to give notice of their approach, shall have <hi type="italic">Holiness to the Lord</hi> upon them," to signify that this is that which we ought to be influenced by ourselves, and make profession of to others, wherever we go. [2.] The furniture of their houses too shall be consecrated to God, to be employed in his service. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The furniture of the priests' houses, or apartments adjoining to the house of the Lord. The common drinking cups they used shall be <hi type="italic">like the bowls before the altar,</hi> that were used either to receive the blood of the sacrifices or to present the wine and oil in, which were for the <hi type="italic">drink-offerings.</hi> The vessels which they used for their own tables shall be used in such a religious manner, with such sobriety and temperance, such devotedness to the glory of God, and such a mixture of pious thoughts and expressions, that their meals shall look like sacrifices; they shall eat and drink, not to themselves, but to him that spreads their tables and fills their cups. And thus, in ministers' families especially, should common actions be done after a godly sort, however they are done in other families. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The furniture of other houses, those of the common people: "<hi type="italic">Every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah shall be holiness to the Lord.</hi> The pots in which they boil their meat, the cups out of which they drink their wine (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.5">Jer. xxxv. 5</reference>), in these God's good creatures shall never be abused to excess, nor that made the food and fuel of lust which should be oil to the wheels of obedience," as had formerly been, when <hi type="italic">all tables were full of vomit and filthiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.8">Isa. xxviii. 8</reference>. "What they eat and drink out of these shall nourish their bodies for the service of God; and out of these they shall give liberally for the relief of the poor;" then are they <hi type="italic">Holiness to the Lord,</hi> as the merchandise and the hire of the converted Tyrians are said to be (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Isa. xxiii. 18</reference>); for both in our gettings and in our spendings we must have an eye to the will of God as our rule and the glory of God as our end. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> When there shall be such an abundance of real holiness people shall not be nice and curious about ceremonial holiness: "<hi type="italic">Those that sacrifice shall come and take</hi> of these common vessels, <hi type="italic">and seethe</hi> their sacrifices <hi type="italic">therein,</hi> making no distinction between them and the <hi type="italic">bowls before the altar.</hi>" In gospel-times the true worshippers shall worship God <hi type="italic">in spirit and in truth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">neither in this mountain nor yet at Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.21">John iv. 21</reference>. One place shall be as acceptable to God as another (<hi type="italic">I will that men pray every where</hi>); and one vessel shall be as acceptable as another. Little regard shall be had to the circumstance, provided there be nothing indecent or disorderly, while the substance is religiously preserved and adhered to. Some think it intimates that there should be greater numbers of sacrifices offered than the vessels of the sanctuary would serve for; but, rather than any should be turned back or deferred, they shall make no difficulty at all of using common vessels, as the Levites in a case of necessity helped the priests to kill the sacrifices, <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.34">2 Chron. xxix. 34</reference>. <div eID="gen21036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21037" type="x-p"/> (2.) There shall be no unholiness introduced into their sacred things, to corrupt them: <hi type="italic">In that day there shall be no more the Canaanite in the house of the Lord of hosts.</hi> Some read it, There shall be no more <hi type="italic">the merchant,</hi> for so a Canaanite sometimes signifies; and they think it was fulfilled when Christ once and again drove the buyers and sellers out of the temple. Or though those that were Canaanites, strangers and foreigners, shall be brought into the house of the Lord, yet they shall cease to be Canaanites; they shall have nothing of the spirit or disposition of Canaanites in them. Or it intimates that though in gospel-times people should grow indifferent as to holy vessels, yet they should be very strict in church-discipline, and careful not to admit the profane to special ordinances, but to separate between the precious and the vile, between Israelites and Canaanites. Yet this will not have its full accomplishment short of the heavenly Jerusalem, that <hi type="italic">house of the Lord of hosts,</hi> into which <hi type="italic">no unclean thing shall enter;</hi> for at the end of time, and not before, Christ shall gather out of his kingdom every thing that offends, and the tares and wheat shall be perfectly and eternally separated.  <chapter eID="Zech.14"/> <div eID="gen21037" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen20752" osisID="Zech" type="book"/>

entries.ff16e4fba5456ceb26d7f7803f6f993e873fd9be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13192"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.14.1-Zech.14.21">Zec 14:1-21</reference>. Last Struggle with the Hostile World-Powers:</title> <div sID="gen24901" type="x-p"/> Messiah-Jehovah Saves Jerusalem and Destroys the Foe, of Whom the Remnant Turns to the Lord Reigning at Jerusalem.<div eID="gen24901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13192"/><hi type="bold">1. day of the Lord--</hi>in which He shall vindicate His justice by punishing the wicked and then saving His elect people (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.31">Joe 2:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">3:14</reference>; Mal 4:1, 5).<div eID="gen24902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy spoil ... divided in the midst of thee--</hi>by the foe; secure of victory, they shall not divide the spoil taken from thee in their camp outside, but "in the midst" of the city itself. <div eID="gen24903" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e075c4ca7102bebb32cb13bfb8121ca8fb267f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13193"/><div sID="gen24904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13193"/><hi type="bold">2. gather all nations, &c.--</hi>The prophecy seems literal (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.2">Joe 3:2</reference>). If Antichrist be the leader of the nations, it seems inconsistent with the statement that he will at this time be sitting in the temple as God at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>); thus Antichrist outside would be made to besiege Antichrist within the city. But difficulties do not set aside revelations: the event will clear up seeming difficulties. Compare the complicated movements, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.1-Dan.11.45">Da 11:1-45</reference>.<div eID="gen24904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">half ... the residue--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">Zec 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>, it is "two-thirds" that perish, and "the third" escapes. There, however, it is "in all the land"; here it is "half of the city." Two-thirds of the "whole people" perish, one-third survives. One-half of the citizens are led captive, the residue are not cut off. Perhaps, too, we ought to translate, "a (not 'the') residue." <div eID="gen24905" type="x-p"/>
entries.31ceee3bf7e254095703f507cc326962415388e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13194"/><div sID="gen24906" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13194"/><hi type="bold">3. Then--</hi>In Jerusalem's extremity.<div eID="gen24906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ... in ... day of battle--</hi>as when Jehovah fought for Israel against the Egyptians at the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.14">Ex 14:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.3">15:3</reference>). As He then made a way through the divided sea, so will He now divide in two "the Mount of Olives" (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.4">Zec 14:4</reference>). <div eID="gen24907" type="x-p"/>
entries.168282a3e7448fedf7c898aeb3c87c8b1e2a63e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13195"/><div sID="gen24908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13195"/>4. The object of the cleaving of the mount in two by a fissure or valley (a prolongation of the valley of Jehoshaphat, and extending from Jerusalem on the west towards Jordan, eastward) is to open a way of escape to the besieged (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.12">Joe 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.14">14</reference>). Half the divided mount is thereby forced northward, half southward; the valley running between. The place of His departure at His ascension shall be the place of His return: and the "manner" of His return also shall be similar (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Ac 1:11</reference>). He shall probably "come from the east" (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.27">Mt 24:27</reference>). He so made His triumphal entry into the city from the Mount of Olives from the east (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.21.10">Mt 21:1-10</reference>). This was the scene of His agony: so it shall be the scene of His glory. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.23">Eze 11:23</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">Eze 43:2</reference>, "from the way of the east." <div eID="gen24908" type="x-p"/>
entries.b03de3b561dc2e1da71ba2688ee6801f49fe581a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13196"/><div sID="gen24909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13196"/><hi type="bold">5. ye shall flee to the valley--</hi>rather "through the valley," as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.29">2Sa 2:29</reference>. The valley made by the cleaving asunder of the Mount of Olives (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.4">Zec 14:4</reference>) is designed to be their way of escape, not their place of refuge [Maurer]. Jerome is on the side of English Version. If it be translated so, it will mean, Ye shall flee "to" the valley, not to hide there, but as the passage through which an escape may be effected. The same divinely sent earthquake which swallows up the foe, opens out a way of escape to God's people. The earthquake in Uzziah's days is mentioned (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Am 1:1</reference>) as a recognized epoch in Jewish history. Compare also <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Is 6:1</reference>: perhaps the same year that Jehovah held His heavenly court and gave commission to Isaiah for the Jews, an earthquake in the physical world, as often happens (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.7">Mt 24:7</reference>), marked momentous movements in the unseen spiritual world.<div eID="gen24909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the mountains--</hi>rather, "of My mountains," namely, Zion and Moriah, peculiarly sacred to Jehovah [Moore]. Or, the mountains formed by My cleaving Olivet into two [Maurer].<div eID="gen24910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Azal--</hi>the name of a place near a gate east of the city. The Hebrew means "adjoining" [Henderson]. Others give the meaning, "departed," "ceased." The valley reaches up to the city gates, so as to enable the fleeing citizens to betake themselves immediately to it on leaving the city.<div eID="gen24911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord my God ... with thee--</hi>The mention of the "Lord my God" leads the prophet to pass suddenly to a direct address to Jehovah. It is as if "lifting up his head" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.28">Lu 21:28</reference>), he suddenly sees in vision the Lord coming, and joyfully exclaims, "All the saints with Thee!" So <reference osisRef="Isa.25.9">Is 25:9</reference>.<div eID="gen24912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saints--</hi>holy angels escorting the returning King (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.30">Mt 24:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">31</reference>; Jude 14); and redeemed men (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">1Co 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.13">1Th 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">4:14</reference>). Compare the similar mention of the "saints" and "angels" at His coming on Sinai (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">De 32:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.53">Ac 7:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Ga 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.2">He 2:2</reference>). Phillips thinks Azal is Ascalon on the Mediterranean. An earthquake beneath Messiah's tread will divide Syria, making from Jerusalem to Azal a valley which will admit the ocean waters from the west to the Dead Sea. The waters will rush down the valley of Arabah, the old bed of the Jordan, clear away the sand-drift of four thousand years, and cause the commerce of Petra and Tyre to center in the holy city. The Dead Sea rising above its shores will overflow by the valley of Edom, completing the straits of Azal into the Red Sea. Thus will be formed the great pool of Jerusalem (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zec 14:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.18">Joe 3:18</reference>). Euphrates will be the north boundary, and the Red Sea the south. Twenty-five miles north and twenty-five miles south of Jerusalem will form one side of the fifty miles square of the Lord's Holy Oblation (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:1-35</reference>). There are seven spaces of fifty miles each from Jerusalem northward to the Euphrates, and five spaces of fifty miles each southward to the Red Sea. Thus there are thirteen equal distances on the breadth of the future promised land, one for the oblation and twelve for the tribes, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:1-35</reference>. That the Euphrates north, Mediterranean west, the Nile and Red Sea south, are to be the future boundaries of the holy land, which will include Syria and Arabia, is favored by <reference osisRef="Gen.15.8">Ge 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.31">Ex 23:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.24">De 11:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.1.4">Jos 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.21">1Ki 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.26">2Ch 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12">Is 27:12</reference>; all which was partially realized in Solomon's reign, shall be antitypically so hereafter. The theory, if true, will clear away many difficulties in the way of the literal interpretation of this chapter and <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:1-35</reference>. <div eID="gen24913" type="x-p"/>
entries.e923f9324fc024f719fa26c56de2cb7b2a1910ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13197"/><div sID="gen24914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13197"/><hi type="bold">6. light ... not ... clear ... dark--</hi>Jerome, Chaldee, Syriac, and Septuagint translate, "There shall not be light, but cold and ice"; that is, a day full of horror (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Am 5:18</reference>). But the Hebrew for "clear" does not mean "cold," but "precious," "splendid" (compare <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>). Calvin translates, "The light shall not be clear, but dark" (literally, "condensation," that is, thick mist); like a dark day in which you can hardly distinguish between day and night. English Version accords with <reference osisRef="Zech.14.7">Zec 14:7</reference>: "There shall not be altogether light nor altogether darkness," but an intermediate condition in which sorrows shall be mingled with joys. <div eID="gen24914" type="x-p"/>
entries.43f5565508463dd2467fe85e3ce7a8fe032a04a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13198"/><div sID="gen24915" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13198"/><hi type="bold">7. one day--</hi>a day altogether unique, different from all others [Maurer]. Compare "one," that is, unique (<reference osisRef="Song.6.9">So 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.7">Jr 30:7</reference>). Not as Henderson explains, "One continuous day, without night" (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.5">Re 22:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.25">21:25</reference>); the millennial period (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.3-Rev.20.7">Re 20:3-7</reference>).<div eID="gen24915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">known to ... Lord--</hi>This truth restrains man's curiosity and teaches us to wait the Lord's own time (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.36">Mt 24:36</reference>).<div eID="gen24916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not day, nor night--</hi>answering to "not ... clear nor ... dark" (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.6">Zec 14:6</reference>); not altogether daylight, yet not the darkness of night.<div eID="gen24917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24918" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at evening ... shall be light--</hi>Towards the close of this twilight-like time of calamity, "light" shall spring up (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.11">Psa 97:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">112:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Is 30:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">60:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen24918" type="x-p"/>
entries.09935445a91470e966ff53d8bd1c8291b42a5cea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13199"/><div sID="gen24919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13199"/><hi type="bold">8. living waters--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.18">Joe 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen24919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">former sea--</hi>that is, the front, or east, which Orientalists face in taking the points of the compass; the Dead Sea.<div eID="gen24920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hinder sea--</hi>the west or Mediterranean.<div eID="gen24921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">summer ... winter--</hi>neither dried up by heat, nor frozen by cold; ever flowing. <div eID="gen24922" type="x-p"/>
entries.65ad19e56925eee03d3c8b04c9d0151d965a5985: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13200"/><div sID="gen24923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13200"/><hi type="bold">9. king over all ... earth--</hi><reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference> implies that this is to be the consequence of Israel being again recognized by God as His own people (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>).<div eID="gen24923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one Lord ... name one--</hi>Not that He is not so already, but He shall then be recognized by all unanimously as "One." Now there are "gods many and lords many." Then Jehovah alone shall be worshipped. The manifestation of the unity of the Godhead shall be simultaneous with that of the unity of the Church. Believers are one in spirit already, even as God is one (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.3-Eph.4.6">Ep 4:3-6</reference>). But externally there are sad divisions. Not until these disappear, shall God reveal fully His unity to the world (<reference osisRef="John.17.21">Joh 17:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.23">23</reference>). Then shall there be "a pure language, that all may call upon the name of the Lord with one consent" (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.9">Zep 3:9</reference>). The Son too shall at last give up His mediatorial kingdom to the Father, when the purposes for which it was established shall have been accomplished, "that God may be all in all" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1Co 15:24</reference>). <div eID="gen24924" type="x-p"/>
entries.16cda9bf2545c17eede73335fa10ac5c0f8fa270: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13201"/><div sID="gen24925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13201"/><hi type="bold">10. turned--</hi>or, "changed round about": literally, "to make a circuit." The whole hilly land round Jerusalem, which would prevent the free passage of the living waters, shall be changed so as to be "as a (or the) plain" (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.4">Is 40:4</reference>).<div eID="gen24925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Geba to Rimmon--</hi>Geba (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.8">2Ki 23:8</reference>) in Benjamin, the north border of Judah. Rimmon, in Simeon (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.32">Jos 15:32</reference>), the south border of Judah; not the Rimmon northeast of Michmash. "The plain from Geba to Rimmon" (that is, from one boundary to the other) is the Arabah or plain of the Jordan, extending from the Sea of Tiberias to the Elanitic Gulf of the Red Sea.<div eID="gen24926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24927" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it shall be lifted up--</hi>namely, Jerusalem shall be exalted, the hills all round being lowered (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.1">Mi 4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen24927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inhabited in her place--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.12.6">Zec 12:6</reference>).<div eID="gen24928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Benjamin's gate--</hi>leading to the territory of Benjamin. The same as Ephraim's gate, the north boundary of the city (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.13">2Ki 14:13</reference>).<div eID="gen24929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the first gate--</hi>west of the city [Grotius]. "The place of," &c. implies that the gate itself was then not in existence. "The old gate" (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.6">Ne 3:6</reference>).<div eID="gen24930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the corner gate--</hi>east of the city [Grotius]. Or the "corner" joining the north and west parts of the wall [Villalpandus]. Grotius thinks "corners" refers to the towers there built (compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.6">Zep 3:6</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen24931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24932" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tower of Hananeel--</hi>south of the city, near the sheep gate (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Ne 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.39">12:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.38">Jr 31:38</reference>) [Grotius].<div eID="gen24932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king's wine-presses--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.8.11">So 8:11</reference>). In the interior of the city, at Zion [Grotius]. <div eID="gen24933" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1a4d66849fa73b34ae4dfc5bec6ed7333c30292: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13202"/><div sID="gen24934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13202"/><hi type="bold">11. no more utter destruction--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.31.40">Jr 31:40</reference>). Literally, "no more curse" (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.3">Re 22:3</reference>; compare Mal 4:6), for there will be no more sin. Temporal blessings and spiritual prosperity shall go together in the millennium: long life (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.20-Isa.65.22">Is 65:20-22</reference>), peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Is 2:4</reference>), honor (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.14-Isa.60.16">Is 60:14-16</reference>), righteous government (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.14">Is 54:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.18">60:18</reference>). Judgment, as usual, begins at the house of God, but then falls fatally on Antichrist, whereon the Church obtains perfect liberty. The last day will end everything evil (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">Ro 8:21</reference>) [Auberlen]. <div eID="gen24934" type="x-p"/>
entries.86879552a39173bd83ea65457edb4b89a6f4f627: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13203"/><div sID="gen24935" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13203"/>12. Punishment on the foe, the last Antichristian confederacy (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.18">Is 59:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.24">66:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.1-Ezek.39.29">Eze 38:1-39:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17-Rev.19.21">Re 19:17-21</reference>). A living death: the corruption (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">Ga 6:8</reference>) of death combined in ghastly union with the conscious sensibility of life. Sin will be felt by the sinner in all its loathsomeness, inseparably clinging to him as a festering, putrid body. <div eID="gen24935" type="x-p"/>
entries.5db0ca8c284534cd268fc7e8e73a4609a90ef34e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13204"/><div sID="gen24936" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13204"/><hi type="bold">13. tumult--</hi>consternation (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.4">Zec 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.15">1Sa 14:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.20">20</reference>).<div eID="gen24936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lay hold ... on ... hand of ... neighbour--</hi>instinctively grasping it, as if thereby to be safer, but in vain [Menochius]. Rather, in order to assail "his neighbor" [Calvin], (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.21">Eze 38:21</reference>). Sin is the cause of all quarrels on earth. It will cause endless quarrels in hell (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.15">Jas 3:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.16">16</reference>). <div eID="gen24937" type="x-p"/>
entries.014e168db3fdee33f8570ebf619e18e22672c434: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13205"/><div sID="gen24938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13205"/><hi type="bold">14. Judah ... fight at Jerusalem--</hi>namely, against the foe: not against Jerusalem, as Maurer translates in variance with the context. As to the spoil gained from the foe, compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.10">Eze 39:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.17">17</reference>. <div eID="gen24938" type="x-p"/>
entries.beb8f4777a7933122f111122af4288657e6bf22e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13206"/><div sID="gen24939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13206"/>15. The plague shall affect the very beasts belonging to the foe. A typical foretaste of all this befell Antiochus Epiphanes and his host at Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 13:49; 2 Maccabees 9:5). <div eID="gen24939" type="x-p"/>
entries.caadc1a74c399e3e65bd50f8d355fa29d95af72d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13207"/><div sID="gen24940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13207"/><hi type="bold">16. every one ... left--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.66.19">Is 66:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">23</reference>). God will conquer all the foes of the Church. Some He will destroy; others He will bring into willing subjection.<div eID="gen24940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from year to year--</hi>literally, "from the sufficiency of a year in a year."<div eID="gen24941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feast of tabernacles--</hi>The other two great yearly feasts, passover and pentecost, are not specified, because, their antitypes having come, the types are done away with. But the feast of tabernacles will be commemorative of the Jews' sojourn, not merely forty years in the wilderness, but for almost two thousand years of their dispersion. So it was kept on their return from the Babylonian dispersion (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.14-Neh.8.17">Ne 8:14-17</reference>). It was the feast on which Jesus made His triumphal entry into Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.8">Mt 21:8</reference>); a pledge of His return to His capital to reign (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">Le 23:34</reference>, 39, 40, 42; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Re 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">21:3</reference>). A feast of peculiar joy (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.15">Psa 118:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.9">Ho 12:9</reference>). The feast on which Jesus gave the invitation to the living waters of salvation ("Hosanna," save us now, was the cry, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.9">Mt 21:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.118.25">Psa 118:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.26">26</reference>) (<reference osisRef="John.7.2">Joh 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.7.37">37</reference>). To the Gentiles, too, it will be significant of perfected salvation after past wanderings in a moral wilderness, as it originally commemorated the ingathering of the harvest. The seedtime of tears shall then have issued in the harvest of joy [Moore]. "All the nations" could not possibly in person go up to the feast, but they may do so by representatives. <div eID="gen24942" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6c696aae7006dbfd454d077852061d90f392c29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13208"/><div sID="gen24943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13208"/><hi type="bold">17. no rain--</hi>including every calamity which usually follows in the East from want of rain, namely, scarcity of provisions, famine, pestilence, &c. Rain is the symbol also of God's favor (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Ho 6:3</reference>). That there shall be unconverted men under the millennium appears from the outbreak of Gog and Magog at the end of it (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.7-Rev.20.9">Re 20:7-9</reference>); but they, like Satan their master, shall be restrained during the thousand years. Note, too, from this verse that the Gentiles shall come up to Jerusalem, rather than the Jews go as missionaries to the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>). However, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.19">Is 66:19</reference> may imply the converse. <div eID="gen24943" type="x-p"/>
entries.fea69a0aaf3231f6674ad9013ae54e024a095fac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13209"/><div sID="gen24944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13209"/><hi type="bold">18. if ... Egypt go not up--</hi>specified as Israel's ancient foe. If Egypt go not up, and so there be no rain on them (a judgment which Egypt would condemn, as depending on the Nile's overflow, not on rain), there shall be the plague ... . Because the guilty are not affected by one judgment, let them not think to escape, for God has other judgments which shall plague them. Maurer translates, "If Egypt go not up, upon them also there shall be none" (no rain). <reference osisRef="Ps.105.32">Psa 105:32</reference> mentions "rain" in Egypt. But it is not their main source of fertility. <div eID="gen24944" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e93359acfe3feacea49c268d231a3aa13be8264: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13210"/><div sID="gen24945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13210"/><hi type="bold">19. punishment--</hi>literally, "sin"; that is, "punishment for sin." <div eID="gen24945" type="x-p"/>
